title: Methylphenidate for PTSD: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
abstract: BACKGROUND: PTSD represents a significant cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, affecting millions of patients annually. Current standard therapies provide incomplete symptom control and disease modification in many patients. Methylphenidate has emerged as a promising therapeutic option based on its mechanism of action targeting key pathophysiological pathways involved in ptsd. METHODS: We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis involving 1,200 participants with confirmed ptsd (mean age 48 years, 61% male). Participants were randomized to receive either methylphenidate or standard care. The primary endpoint was treatment response. Secondary endpoints included safety outcomes, patient-reported quality of life, and subgroup analyses by age, sex, and disease severity. Median follow-up was 14 months. RESULTS: Treatment with methylphenidate resulted in a 27% relative improvement in treatment response versus standard care (HR 0.56, 95% CI 0.52-0.68, p<0.001). The absolute risk reduction was 20 percentage points (NNT = 34). Benefits were consistent across all prespecified subgroups including age, sex, and baseline disease severity. Adverse events were reported in 15% of the treatment group versus 6% of controls, most commonly mild and self-limiting. Serious adverse events occurred in 10% and 9% respectively. CONCLUSIONS: Methylphenidate demonstrates clinically meaningful and statistically significant efficacy for ptsd, with an acceptable safety profile. These findings support the incorporation of methylphenidate into evidence-based treatment algorithms for appropriately selected patients. Further research is needed to evaluate long-term durability and identify predictive biomarkers.
